{{Short description|Molecular animator}}
'''Janet Iwasa''' is an American [[data visualization]] expert and [[associate professor]] of [[biochemistry]] at the [[University of Utah]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-01-15 |title=Janet Iwasa {{!}} School of Medicine |url=https://medicine.utah.edu/faculty/janet-iwasa |access-date=2024-01-06 |website=medicine.utah.edu |language=en}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
In 1978, Janet Iwasa was born to parents Mikeko and Kuni Iwasa in [[Bloomington, Indiana|Bloomington]], Indiana. She was the youngest of three children.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Iwasa|first=Janet|title=Karp's Cell and Molecular Biology|publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]]|year=2020|isbn=978-1119598244|pages=5|language=English}}</ref> Following her father joining the [[National Institutes of Health]], she moved, with her family,  to Maryland.<ref name=Reynolds>{{Cite web|last=Reynolds|first=Sharon|title=Meeting Janet Iwasa |date=15 August 2014 |url=https://biobeat.nigms.nih.gov/2014/08/meet-janet-iwasa/ |access-date=2017-12-08}}</ref><ref name="Fleichman">Fleichman, John (February 2009). "[http://www.ascb.org/files/0902profile.pdf ASCB Profile: Janet Iwasa]" (PDF). ASCB Newsletter: 39–41. Retrieved 10 December 2017.</ref> She later went on to  participate in an internship at the [[J. Craig Venter Institute|Institute for Genomic Research]].<ref name=Reynolds />

In 1999, she graduated ''with great honor'' from [[Williams College]] with bachelor's degrees in Biology and Asian Studies.<ref name=":2">Janet Iwasa, Ph.D., University of Utah, [https://biochem.web.utah.edu/iwasa/bio.html Curriculum Vita]</ref> In her junior year at Williams, she worked alongside  Professor Robert Savage, studying the formation of segmented patterns in leeches on a cellular level.<ref>''rpsci98 - BIOLOGY DEPARTMENT'', https://science.williams.edu/wp-content/blogs.dir/72/files/RS98html/RepSci98Web-BIOLOGY.html.</ref> In 2006, Iwasa obtained a PhD in [[cell biology]] at the [[University of California, San Francisco|University of California]] in San Francisco. She wrote her doctoral thesis on the topic of [[Actin|actin networks]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Iwasa|first=Janet|date=June 21, 2006|title=Spatial and Temporal Relationships between Actin-Filament Nucleation, Capping, and Disassembly|url=https://www.cell.com/current-biology/pdf/S0960-9822(07)00987-6.pdf|access-date=October 28, 2021|website=Cell}}</ref>

After watching a molecular animation by [[Graham Johnson (scientist)|Graham Johnson]], she began to pursue 3D animation. She began taking animation classes at [[San Francisco State University]].<ref name=Reynolds /><ref name=":3">Iwasa, Janet H. "Crafting a Career in Molecular Animation." ''Molecular Biology of the Cell'', vol. 25, no. 19, 29 Oct. 2014, pp. 2891–2893. ''NCBI'', {{doi|10.1091/mbc.e14-01-0699}}.</ref> After graduation, she studied animation at the [[Gnomon School of Visual Effects]] in [[Hollywood, Los Angeles|Hollywood]], California; she was the only woman in her class. She applied her skills in animation to biology, using 3D animation as a means to visualize cellular functions and interactions.<ref name=Reynolds />

== Career and research ==
In 2006, Iwasa began working as a [[postdoctoral]] fellow under [[Jack W. Szostak|Jack Szostak]] with [[Harvard University]] and the Massachusetts General Hospital.<ref name=":2" /><ref>"Szostak Lab: [http://molbio.mgh.harvard.edu/szostakweb/past.html Former Post-Doctoral Fellows]". Molecular Biology. Harvard Medical School. Retrieved 10 December 2017.</ref> In 2007, Iwasa worked as a teaching assistant at [[Harvard Medical School]], in the "Visualizing Molecular Processes with Maya" course.<ref name=":2" /> She also worked with [[MASSIVE (software)|MASSIVE]], adapting the visual effects software to depict processes of nucleation elongation.<ref name="Fleichman" />

In 2008, Iwasa created illustrations and animations for a multimedia exhibit for the [[Museum of Science (Boston)|Boston Museum of Science]] titled ''Exploring Life's Origins''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=About the Exploring Origins Project|url=https://exploringorigins.org/about.html|website=Exploring Life's Origins}}</ref>

In 2008, she became a lecturer in Molecular Visualization for the Department of Cell Biology at [[Harvard Medical School]].<ref name=":2" /> Her work with Joan Brugge and Michael Overholtzer furthered her understanding of a newly discovered cellular process called endosis. Iwasa worked alongside researchers at the university to investigate the process.<ref name="Fleichman" />

While working with Tomas Kirchausen, she created an animation on [[clathrin-mediated endocytosis]], researching how [[clathrin triskelion]]s operated and assembled on the inner surface of the plasma membrane to invaginate an extracellular particle.<ref name="Fleichman" /><ref name=":3" />

In 2010, Iwasa organized and taught a course on visualizing molecular and cellular processes with 3D animation in Porto, Portugal.<ref>{{Cite web|title=News — The Animation Lab|url=https://animationlab.utah.edu/news|access-date=October 28, 2021|website=The Animation Lab}}</ref> In 2013, she joined the [[University of Utah School of Medicine]] as a research assistant professor for the Department of Cell Biology. She returned to Portugal in 2014 to teach a 3D animation workshop for scientific animation.<ref name=":2" /> In 2014, she also completed a project called Molecular Flipbook,<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://molecularflipbook.org/ | title=Molecular Flipbook}}</ref> a free, open-source software program designed to animate molecules. In 2016, Iwasa released a life-cycle animation on [[HIV/AIDS|HIV]]. Her project used animation to illustrate the molecular mechanisms the virus utilizes to enter into and exit target cells.<ref>Iwasa, Janet. [https://biochem.web.utah.edu/iwasa/projects/HIV.html "Visualizing HIV Entry and Egress."]</ref><ref name=":3" />. 

In addition to teaching and her research, Iwasa directs the Animation Lab at the University of Utah. The lab focuses on developing high quality molecular and cellular animations that help scientists that communicate complex biological processes. Through collaboration with researchers, the lab creates visualizations of molecular mechanisms that are difficult to observe directly. this process helps improve scientific education and public understanding of cellular biology.<ref>{{Cite web |author-link= |title=The Animation Lab |url=https://animationlab.utah.edu/ |access-date=2026-03-16 |website=The Animation Lab |language=en-US}}</ref>

Iwasa is a [[TED (conference)|TED]] senior fellow, and has spoken about animation in molecular biology at both TED and TEDx conferences. She has also contributed to TED-Ed.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Iwasa |first=Janet |title=Janet Iwasa {{!}} Speaker {{!}} TED |url=https://www.ted.com/speakers/janet_iwasa |access-date=2024-02-05 |website=www.ted.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Iwasa |first=Janet |title=Why it's so hard to cure HIV/AIDS |date=2017-09-07 |url=https://www.ted.com/talks/janet_iwasa_why_it_s_so_hard_to_cure_hiv_aids |access-date=2024-02-05}}</ref>

=== Publications ===
Iwasa's work has been published in scientific journals including ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'', ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'', and ''[[Cell (journal)|Cell]]'', as well as the ''[[New York Times]]''.<ref>Olsen, Erik (15 November 2010). "[https://www.nytimes.com/2010/11/16/science/16animate.html Molecular Animation: Where Cinema and Biology Meet]". ''The New York Times''. Retrieved 10 December 2017.</ref><ref>"Janet Iwasa". [https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/the-secret-life-of-scientists-and-engineers-janet-iwasa/ Secret Life of Scientists and Engineers]. PBS. Retrieved 10 December 2017.</ref>

Iwasa's knowledge of cellular animation has also led her to publish several different works of scientific literature. Her work with Robert Savage's Lab led to her first publication in 1999 in ''Development Genes and Evolution'', "The leech hunchback protein is expressed in the [[epithelium]] and [[Central nervous system|CNS]] but not in the segmental precursor lineages", with co-authors Suver and Savage.<ref name=":0">Iwasa, J. H, et al. "The Leech Hunchback Protein Is Expressed in the Epithelium and CNS but Not in the Segmental Precursor Lineages." ''Development Genes and Evolution'', vol. 210, no. 6, 19 May 2000, pp. 277–288. ''Springer Nature '', {{doi|10.1007/s004270050315}}.</ref> Iwasa's work with Savage focused on identifying regulatory genes engaged in the formation of segment patterns in annelids, investigating a gene in leeches called Leech Zinc Finger II (LZF2), considered to be an [[Sequence homology|orthologue]] of the ''hunchback (hb)'' gene in ''[[Drosophila]]''. Iwasa, Savage, and Suver concluded that LZF2 likely plays an important part in the morphological progressions of [[gastrulation]] and the specification of the central nervous system in leeches but does not contribute to the formation of [[Anatomical terms of location|anteroposterior]] patterns.<ref name=":0" />

In 2007, she published an article on her research at the University of California with Mullins, "Spatial and temporal relationships between actin-filament nucleation, capping, and disassembly."<ref name=":1">Iwasa JH, Mullins RD. Spatial and temporal relationships between actin-filament nucleation, capping, and disassembly. [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17331727 Curr Biol]. 2007 Mar 6; 17(5):395-406</ref> Her study with Mullins focused on the [[Lamellipodium|lamellipodial]] network. They concluded that the lamellipodial network incorporates the [[Arp2/3 complex|Arp 2/3 complex]] and [[Capping protein (actin filament) muscle Z-line, alpha 1|capping proteins]] during initial assembly, but dismisses these complexes long before the lamellipodial network is actually disassembled. They also reported that the network does not use [[cofilin]], twinfilin, and [[tropomyosin]] in assembly. Instead, these factors play a role in the network's size.<ref name=":1" />

In 2010, she published "Animating the model figure" in ''Trends in Cell Biology.''<ref name=":4">Iwasa JH (2010). [http://www.cell.com/trends/cell-biology/fulltext/S0962-8924(10)00155-8 Animating the model figure]. ''Trends Cell Biol'', ''20''(12), 699-704.</ref> In this article, she points out the importance of animations in revealing and teaching scientific concepts, explaining that students are shown to retain more information and show more interest in the material when animations are incorporated into the curriculum. She also pushed the invention of animation software engineered exclusively for the scientific research community.<ref name=":4" />

In 2015, Iwasa and Wallace Marshal co-authored ''Karp's Cell and Molecular Biology: Concepts and Experiments'' by Gerald Karp''.''<ref>Iwasa, JH and Marshall, W (December 2015). ''[http://www.wiley.com/WileyCDA/WileyTitle/productCd-EHEP003376.html Karp's Cell Biology] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201080819/http://www.wiley.com/WileyCDA/WileyTitle/productCd-EHEP003376.html |date=2017-12-01 }}: Concepts and Experiments'' (8). Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley and Sons, Inc.</ref>

In 2016, Iwasa published "The Scientist as Illustrator" in ''Trends in Immunology'', in which she describes the role of animation in science and discusses the importance of visualization.<ref name=":5">Iwasa JH (2016). "[http://www.cell.com/trends/immunology/fulltext/S1471-4906(16)00022-3 The Scientist as Illustrator]". ''Trends Immunol'', ''37''(4), 247-50.</ref>

== Recognition and honors ==
From 1999 to 2004, Iwasa was honoured as a member of the NSF Graduate Fellowship. From 2006 to 2008, she was a member of the NSF Discpery Corps Postgraduate Fellowship.<ref name=":2" /> In 2008, she earned an honourable mention for her entry into the AAAS International Science & Engineering Visualization Challenge. In 2012, she was listed as one of ''[[Fast Company (magazine)|Fast Company]]''{{'}}s "100 Most Creative People."<ref name=":2" /><ref>Cain, Patrick (27 April 2012). "[https://www.fastcompany.com/3018210/25-janet-iwasa 100 Most Creative People]: 25. Janet Iwasa". Fast Company. Retrieved 11 December 2017.</ref> In 2014, she was recognized as a [[TED Fellow]], a FASEB BioArt Winner, and one of ''[[Foreign Policy Magazine]]''{{'}}s "100 Leading Global Thinkers."<ref name=":2" /><ref>"Janet Iwasa". [https://www.ted.com/speakers/janet_iwasa TED Speakers]. TED.com. Retrieved 11 December 2017.</ref><ref>"Foreign Policy Unveils Sixth Annual "[https://fpgroup.foreignpolicy.com/foreign-policy-unveils-sixth-annual-100-leading-global-thinkers-issue/ 100 Leading Global Thinkers]" Issue". Foreign Policy Group. 17 November 2014. Retrieved 11 December 2017.</ref> In 2016, the University of Utah credited Iwasa as an Entrepreneurial Faculty Scholar. In 2017, she was honoured as a TED Senior Fellow.<ref name=":2" />

Iwasa has also played an important role in promoting the use of scientific visualization in education. Through workshops, lectures, and online educational platforms, she has encouraged scientists and students to use animation as a tool to better explain biological processes. Her work highlights how visual storytelling can make complex molecular mechanisms more accessible to both researchers and the public.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Iwasa |first=Janet |author-link= |date=February 2023 |title=Janet Iwasa |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2022.12.022 |journal=Current Biology |volume=33 |issue=3 |pages=R87–R89 |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2022.12.022 |issn=0960-9822}}</ref>

In 2012, Iwasa was ranked 25th in the "100 most creative people" by FastCompany.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2012-04-27 |title=25. Janet Iwasa |url=https://www.fastcompany.com/3018210/25-janet-iwasa |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230107130651/https://www.fastcompany.com/3018210/25-janet-iwasa |archive-date=2023-01-07 |access-date=2026-03-16 |work=Fast Company |language=en-US}}</ref>
